title: Design Patterns in C++
summary: Use the patterns real C++ is built from: scope guards, strategies at run time and compile time, factories, observers, and pimpl, and see why singletons hurt.
intro: A design pattern is a named shape for code that solves a problem that keeps coming back: undo a change however a function exits, swap one algorithm for another, build the right class from a name in a config file, tell every interested part of a program that a price moved. The names let a team discuss a design in one word, and C++ gives each pattern its own twist, from destructors to templates. You will build the patterns trading code uses most, and for each one see what it costs and when it is worth it.

steps.title: RAII beyond memory: scope guards

example.title: Pause trading during a reload
example.prompt: Turn trading off while a config reloads, and let a scope guard turn it back on after a normal return, an early return, and an exception.
example.output:
reloading v2
  loaded v2
  trading resumed
reloading v2
  already loaded
  trading resumed
reloading v-1
  trading resumed
  error: bad version
trading on: true
example.explanation: `resume` is created right after the flag goes off, so every way out of `reload` destroys it and runs the lambda. The first call returns at the end, the second returns early, and the third throws. On the throw, the guard's destructor runs during stack unwinding, before the `catch` in `main`, which is why `trading resumed` prints before the error. No path can leave trading off, and `reload` never repeats the cleanup by hand.

practice.title: Halt a symbol while its limits change
practice.prompt:
Halt trading in a symbol while its maximum order size changes, and let a scope guard lift the halt on every path.

1. Give `ScopeGuard` a destructor that calls `cleanup_`.
2. At the top of `update`, set `limits.halted` to true and create a guard whose lambda sets it back to false and prints `  resumed` (two spaces first).
3. Leave the rest of `update` and `main` as they are.

Input:

```text
3
250
250
0
```

Expected output:

```text
updating to 250
  max 250
  resumed
updating to 250
  unchanged
  resumed
updating to 0
  resumed
  error: max must be positive
halted: false
```

tests.output:
updating to 250
  max 250
  resumed
updating to 250
  unchanged
  resumed
updating to 0
  resumed
  error: max must be positive
halted: false

updating to 100
  unchanged
  resumed
halted: false

updating to -5
  resumed
  error: max must be positive
updating to 40
  max 40
  resumed
halted: false

hints: The destructor is one line: `~ScopeGuard() { cleanup_(); }`.
Capture `limits` by reference in the lambda, as the example captures `engine`: `[&limits] { ... }`.
Name the guard, as in `ScopeGuard resume(...)`. Without a name it is destroyed at once and prints `  resumed` too early.

steps.title: Strategy and factory

example.title: Sizing rules from a config
example.prompt: Build sizing rules by name with a factory, use them through the base class, and size one more order through a template with no virtual call.
example.output:
fixed: 300 shares at 125
cash: 40 shares at 125
kelly: unknown rule
template: 125 shares at 40
example.explanation: The loop only knows `SizingRule`. `makeRule` reads each name, picks the derived class, and returns it as a `std::unique_ptr<SizingRule>`, or `nullptr` for `kelly`, which the loop reports and skips. Each `rule->size(125.0)` is a virtual call that lands in `FixedQty` or `FixedCash`. `CashRule` has no base and no `virtual`: `sizeOrder(CashRule{5000}, 40.0)` stamps out a copy of the template for `CashRule`, where the call goes to one known function the compiler can inline. Both cash rules use `static_cast<int>`, which truncates, so they never buy more than the cash covers.

practice.title: Fee models by name
practice.prompt:
Pick fee models by name with a factory, and price one more fee through a template.

1. Override `fee` in `FlatFee` to return `amount_`, and in `BpsFee` to return `notional * bps_ / 10000`.
2. Finish `makeFee`: `flat` makes a `FlatFee`, `bps` makes a `BpsFee`, and any other name returns `nullptr`.
3. Write `template <typename Model> double feeFor(const Model& model, double notional)` that returns `model.fee(notional)`.
4. Read a notional and `n`, then `n` lines of `name param`. For each, print `<name>: fee <fee>`, or `<name>: unknown model` when the factory returns `nullptr`.
5. Last, print `template: fee <fee>` for `HalfBps{}` through `feeFor`. Every fee has 2 decimals.

Input:

```text
10000
3
flat 1.50
bps 2
maker 1
```

Expected output:

```text
flat: fee 1.50
bps: fee 2.00
maker: unknown model
template: fee 0.50
```

tests.output:
flat: fee 1.50
bps: fee 2.00
maker: unknown model
template: fee 0.50

bps: fee 7.50
flat: fee 0.00
template: fee 12.50

hints: Copy the base signature and add `override`: `double fee(double notional) const override { ... }`. FlatFee can leave the parameter unnamed, as `FixedQty::size` does.
In `makeFee`, `if (name == "flat") { return std::make_unique<FlatFee>(param); }`, then the same for `bps`.
Test the factory's result with `if (!model)` before you call `model->fee(notional)`.

steps.title: Observer: notifying subscribers

example.title: A quote feed with two listeners
example.prompt: Publish quotes to a logger and a price alert through one listener interface, then unsubscribe the logger.
example.output:
log AAPL 100.50
log AAPL 101.25
alert AAPL above 101.00
alert AAPL above 101.00
example.explanation: `QuoteFeed` only knows the `QuoteListener` interface, so it calls `onQuote` on a `Logger` and a `PriceAlert` alike, in the order they subscribed. The second quote reaches both, the logger first. `unsubscribe` uses erase and remove, as in *Lambdas and STL Algorithms*, so the last quote only reaches the alert. `logger` and `alert` are declared before `feed`, and locals are destroyed in reverse order, so the feed is gone before its listeners and can never call a dead one.

practice.title: Fill listeners
practice.prompt:
Send fills to a position tracker and a big fill alert, and let the input mute the alert.

1. Finish `FillFeed::publish` so it calls `onFill` on every listener in subscription order.
2. Finish `FillFeed::unsubscribe` with erase and `std::remove`.
3. Override `onFill` in `BigFillAlert` to print `big fill <symbol> <qty>` when `qty` is at least `threshold_`.
4. `main` is done: it reads `n` commands, each `fill <symbol> <qty>` or `mute`, which unsubscribes the alert.

Input:

```text
4
fill AAPL 100
fill AAPL 500
mute
fill AAPL 600
```

Expected output:

```text
position 100
position 600
big fill AAPL 500
position 1200
```

tests.stdin:
4
fill AAPL 100
fill AAPL 500
mute
fill AAPL 600
tests.output:
position 100
position 600
big fill AAPL 500
position 1200

tests.stdin:
3
fill MSFT 900
fill MSFT -900
fill MSFT 499
tests.output:
position 900
big fill MSFT 900
position 0
position 499

hints: `publish` is the loop from the example: `for (FillListener* listener : listeners_) { listener->onFill(symbol, qty); }`.
`unsubscribe` is one line: `listeners_.erase(std::remove(listeners_.begin(), listeners_.end(), listener), listeners_.end());`.
`BigFillAlert::onFill` must match the base exactly: `void onFill(const std::string& symbol, int qty) override`.

steps.title: Pimpl, and the trouble with singletons

example.title: An engine behind a pointer
example.prompt: Hide an engine's members behind a pimpl, with the header part, the implementation part, and the code that uses it marked as the three files they would be.
example.explanation: The header part declares `struct Impl;` without defining it, which is enough to hold a `std::unique_ptr<Impl>`. Only the implementation part defines `Impl` and needs `<vector>`. Every member function reaches the data through `impl_->`. `Engine::~Engine() = default;` comes after `Impl` is complete, so the `std::unique_ptr` knows how to delete it. `sizeof(Engine)` is 8, one pointer, and stays 8 however many members `Impl` gains, so code compiled against the header never has to change. Here all three parts share one file, so `Impl` is complete before `main` either way. Split into real files, only this order lets `main.cpp` destroy an `Engine`.

practice.title: A price cache behind a pimpl
practice.prompt:
Implement a price cache whose header shows nothing but a pointer.

1. Define `struct PriceCache::Impl` holding a `std::map<std::string, double>` of last prices.
2. Define the constructor, which makes the `Impl` with `std::make_unique`, and the destructor as `= default`.
3. Define `update`, `last` (which returns 0.0 for a symbol never seen), and `symbols`, the number of symbols stored.
4. In `main`, read `n`, then `n` lines of `symbol price`, and update the cache with each. Then read one query symbol.
5. Print `<query> <last price>` with 2 decimals, then `symbols <count>`, then the `sizeof(PriceCache)` line the starter already prints.

Input:

```text
3
AAPL 189.84
MSFT 411.22
AAPL 190.10
AAPL
```

Expected output:

```text
AAPL 190.10
symbols 2
sizeof(PriceCache) 8
```
hints: Start the implementation part with `struct PriceCache::Impl { std::map<std::string, double> lastPrice; };`, then `PriceCache::PriceCache() : impl_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}`.
`last` is `const`, so look the symbol up with `find` instead of `[]`, which would insert it.
Every member function reaches the map through `impl_->lastPrice`, as the example reaches `impl_->position`.

recap:
- RAII is the core pattern: a destructor undoes what a constructor did, on every path out of a scope. A `ScopeGuard` holding a lambda covers one-off cleanups. Name it and delete its copies.
- Strategy puts an algorithm behind an interface. A virtual base lets you choose at run time, and a template parameter fixes the choice at compile time so the call can inline.
- A factory turns data such as a config name into a `std::unique_ptr<Base>`, or `nullptr` for an unknown name, so the rest of the code only sees the base. Holding the rule as a member is composition.
- Observer: a subject calls every subscribed listener through an interface, in subscription order. Listeners must outlive the subject or unsubscribe, or the subject calls through a dangling pointer.
- Pimpl hides private members in a struct only the `.cpp` defines, so changing them rebuilds one file. Declare the destructor in the header and define it in the `.cpp`.
- A singleton is a global with extra steps. A function-local static fixes the initialization order, but testing and hidden dependencies still suffer, so prefer passing one object by reference.

That ends the More Object-Oriented Programming section. Next, **Sorting with Comparators** opens the Data Structures and Algorithms section, the classic algorithms built on the containers you know, starting with sorting by your own rules.
